design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled two-period crossover trial (NCT02541422) at a US level 1 trauma centre: 49 healthy adults who completed both sessions drank beer under supervision to a set breath alcohol level and were given N-acetylcysteine (NAC) or identical lactose placebo capsules (doses and timing in the exposure field), the other treatment at the second session; the next morning they rated hangover symptoms at home on the Hangover Symptoms Scale. Primary outcome total symptom score; secondary headache, nausea, weakness and a comparison by sex. The PubMed Central version includes an author correction to the Introduction (Sci Rep 2021;11:15262).
can_establish: Whether NAC capsules taken during a supervised session of beer drinking, at the low doses and the one timing used (exposure field), made a large difference to next-morning hangover symptom scores in healthy young adults, compared with placebo in the same people.
cannot_establish: Whether NAC has a small or moderate effect (no intervals reported; medians only), whether higher doses or other timing would differ, whether the apparent benefit in women is real (a subgroup comparison among several tests, called post hoc in the Discussion, with men faring worse on NAC), and whether results hold for longer, unsupervised drinking without a fixed stopping point, or for drinking after leaving the site, which was not controlled.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers aged over 21 at St. Luke's University Health Network, Pennsylvania; how they were recruited is not described. Predominantly white; most aged 20 to 30 according to the Limitations.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults over 21 without alcohol use disorder (self-report). Excluded: diabetes, kidney or bladder stones, kidney or liver disease, stomach ulcers, organ transplant or dialysis, allergy to alcohol, egg, milk or wheat, pregnancy (urine test), and a list of medications (including several antibiotics, carbamazepine, nitroglycerine and activated charcoal).
sample.demographics: 31 men and 18 women, predominantly white, mostly 20 to 30 years old; no means or SDs reported.
sample.attrition: 62 enrolled, 49 completed (13 lost, 21%): scheduling conflicts (number not given), one could not tolerate the amount of beer, one withdrew; analysis of completers only. The five-item analysis in Table 1 has 91 observations (45 NAC, 46 placebo) instead of 98, without explanation.
sample.selection_effects: Young, mostly white volunteers willing to drink to intoxication twice in a hospital setting; completers only.

exposure.measurement: Supervised drinking of the same beer, one bottle at a time, with breath alcohol measured 15 minutes after each until the target was reached; capsules given by staff, with vapour rub under the nose to mask the capsule's smell.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: 12 oz beers of 5.2% alcohol by volume until breath alcohol reached 0.1 g/210 L (plus or minus 0.005), in sessions starting in the early afternoon; then one, two or three capsules of 600 mg NAC or lactose placebo by mouth, according to the number of beers drunk (1 to 3, 4 to 6, 7 or more). Participants stayed until breath alcohol was below 0.08 g/210 L and were driven home; drinking after leaving was not controlled. The interval between the two sessions is not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Listed interacting medications excluded; smoking and other drug use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; symptoms were rated within an hour of waking the next morning, unsupervised.

comparison.controls: The same participants after identical-looking lactose placebo capsules at the other session, drinking to the same breath alcohol target.
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover; order assigned by random number generator by a person who kept the allocation from the investigators.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant within person. Number of beers per session, sleep and drinking after leaving the site were not reported or not controlled.

outcomes.instruments: Hangover Symptoms Scale (Slutske et al., 2003): 13 symptoms rated on a five-point agreement scale (thirst, tiredness, headache, nausea, vomiting, weakness, difficulty concentrating, sensitivity to light and sound, sweating, trouble sleeping, anxiety, depression, trembling); a general hangover visual analogue scale (results not reported); and a subset of five items described as valid, summed.
outcomes.validity_norms: The paper calls the scale previously verified (validated in college students) in the Limitations, and technically not validated in the Methods, where it adds the five-item subset for that reason.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcome: total symptom score, NAC against placebo within person. Secondary: headache, nausea and weakness; difference scores (NAC minus placebo) compared between women and men.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants and investigators blinded; capsules identical; smell masked. Symptoms were self-rated at home without supervision.

analysis.effect_sizes: Medians only, no intervals: total score NAC 10 against placebo 13 (P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum score); headache 1 against 1 (P = 0.93); nausea 0 against 1 (P = 0.11); weakness 1 against 1 (P = 0.72); five-item subset 5 (range 0 to 19) against 5.5 (0 to 20), P = 0.86. Difference scores (NAC minus placebo) by sex: women −3.5, men +2 (P = 0.04); nausea P = 0.05, weakness P = 0.03, headache P = 0.32.
analysis.covariates: None; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for NAC against placebo, Mann-Whitney tests for sex comparisons and for the five-item subset.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02541422, registered 4 September 2015 according to the paper. The registry record was not read, so registered and reported outcomes were not compared.
analysis.selective_reporting: The general hangover visual analogue scale is described but no result is given. The Discussion calls the symptom-specific comparisons post hoc, while the Methods list headache, nausea, weakness and the sex comparison as secondary outcomes. The legend of Figure 1 says the results suggest benefit in people with high alcohol intake or high symptom scores, an analysis that is not reported anywhere.
analysis.power: Calculated in advance (PASS 11): 41 participants for a 20% reduction at alpha 0.05 and 90% power; 49 completed. The variability assumed is not stated. A survey of 69 medical professionals put the smallest clinically meaningful reduction at 69.4%.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 49 young adults, NAC capsules taken during supervised beer drinking did not change next-morning hangover symptoms detectably compared with placebo (median totals 10 against 13 out of 52; P = 0.45), nor headache, nausea or weakness. Comparing difference scores by sex, women scored lower on NAC than placebo (median −3.5) and men higher (+2), P = 0.04, with no correction for the several tests. Side effects were few and mild on both NAC and placebo.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusion say the study was "suggestive of gender specific susceptibility" with women's symptoms improved after NAC. Gaps: (1) the primary outcome was null, and the sex difference is a subgroup comparison among several uncorrected tests that the Discussion itself calls post hoc for the individual symptoms; (2) the abstract does not say that men scored worse on NAC than on placebo; (3) the Figure 1 legend asserts benefit in people with high alcohol intake or high symptom scores without any reported analysis; (4) the title speaks of prevention, but when the capsules were taken (exposure field) limits what prevention can mean here. The Limitations are candid about dose, timing of drinking and self-administration of the scale.

timeline.event: Results presented as posters at three conferences.
Full report published; an author correction the next month replaced an inaccurate passage on ethanol metabolism in the Introduction and one reference, with no change to methods or results.

replication.where_it_stands: A single small trial of NAC for hangover. The authors cite an earlier trial of an L-cysteine-containing supplement (Eriksson et al., 2020) as positive; that is a different product and was not read here.

funding.funder: In part, a research scholarship from the St. Luke's University Health Network Women's Auxiliary Group.
funding.declared_conflicts: The corresponding author has recently begun consulting for Galephar Pharmaceuticals on a hangover medication, which she states started years after the study was completed; no other conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors from St. Luke's University Health Network; the drinking protocol was the same as in another study by the same group (Kelly et al., 2020).

what_would_settle_it: A larger preregistered randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial with a validated hangover severity scale as the primary outcome, a prespecified test of the treatment-by-sex interaction, more than one dose, realistic drinking sessions with sleep recorded and no unmonitored drinking afterwards, and effect sizes with confidence intervals.

domains.note: Order assigned by random number generator; allocation kept from investigators by the person assigning treatments.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: NAC is short-acting, so carryover is unlikely, but the interval between sessions is not reported and period effects were not examined; the number of beers needed to reach the target in each period is not reported.
Blinding was well designed (identical capsules, smell masked). Drinking after leaving the site was not controlled, as the authors note, and could differ between periods.
13 of 62 enrolled (21%) did not complete, mostly for scheduling, and only completers were analysed; 7 of 98 expected observations are missing from the five-item analysis without explanation.
Blinded self-ratings on an established symptom scale; completed at home within an hour of waking without supervision, which adds noise but not bias between conditions.

Registered, but the registry was not checked here; the five-item re-scoring, the unreported visual analogue scale, and a figure legend asserting an unreported analysis suggest flexible analysis around the null primary result.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomization, concealment and blinding were done well, so the null primary result is credible as far as its precision allows; concerns come from completers-only analysis with 21% loss, unreported session interval, uncontrolled drinking after leaving, and analyses beyond the primary outcome that are inconsistently described. The card may be cited for no detectable effect of NAC on next-morning symptom scores at these doses and this timing. It should not be cited for a benefit in women: that comparison is a subgroup test among several, with men scoring worse on NAC, and the analysis treats the sex difference rather than testing an interaction prespecified with adequate power.

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome: total Hangover Symptoms Scale score did not differ between NAC and placebo (median 10 against 13, P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum score) in 49 completers.
key_findings.note: The percentages correspond to a maximum of 52 (13 items scored 0 to 4), while the Methods describe items scored 1 to 5 (editors' arithmetic).

key_findings.finding: Secondary symptoms did not differ: headache median 1 against 1 (P = 0.93), nausea 0 against 1 (P = 0.11), weakness 1 against 1 (P = 0.72); the five-item subset 5 (0 to 19) against 5.5 (0 to 20), P = 0.86.

By sex, the difference score (NAC minus placebo) was −3.5 in women and +2 in men (P = 0.04), with sex differences for nausea (P = 0.05) and weakness (P = 0.03) but not headache (P = 0.32); the Discussion calls the symptom comparisons post hoc.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Side effects participants attributed to the pill: after NAC, gastrointestinal symptoms (4), headache (2), rash (1), muscle twitches (1) and insomnia (1); after placebo, headache (3) and gastrointestinal symptoms (1); no serious adverse events.
62 participants were enrolled and 49 completed (31 men, 18 women, predominantly white); losses were mostly for scheduling, one could not tolerate the beer and one withdrew.

The authors name as limitations that the low doses may have been below a therapeutic level, that the supervised sessions, which ended at a breath alcohol target, may have produced milder hangovers than unrestricted drinking, that participants may have drunk more after leaving, and that the scale was self-administered without supervision.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods describe each symptom rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), which with 13 items gives a minimum total of 13; the reported median totals of 10 and 13 and the percentages of 19% and 25% of the maximum match items scored 0 to 4 (maximum 52), as in the sample-size section.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 5th paragraph; Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Scores should be described on the 0 to 52 scale; the Methods description is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 compares NAC with placebo, and women with men, using Mann-Whitney tests for independent groups, although each participant contributed to both conditions; its sample sizes (45 and 46; 34 women and 57 men) do not match 49 completers in two periods (98 observations; 36 and 62).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1 and its footnote; Methods, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The five-item analysis ignores the paired design and has unexplained missing observations.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 1 legend states that the results suggest improvement in people with high alcohol intake or high symptom scores; no such analysis is reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a finding of this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls the symptom-specific sex differences post hoc, while the Methods name headache, nausea, weakness and the sex comparison as secondary outcomes.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 7th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether these analyses were planned is unclear; they should be treated as exploratory.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the scale is technically not validated, the Limitations that it was previously verified in college students; and the Limitations say participants mostly ranged from 20 to 30 years, although only people over 21 were eligible.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods, 6th paragraph; Limitations, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The general hangover visual analogue scale is described in the Methods but its results are not reported.
